title: Maximum Heart Rate by Age Calculator | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Calculate Your Maximum Heart Rate by Age
description: ❤️ Calculate your maximum heart rate using the Tanaka formula (208 − 0.7×age). More accurate than 220-age. Fast, free, and instant.
intro: Maximum heart rate (HRmax) is the ceiling your heart can reach during all-out exertion, measured in beats per minute (bpm). It anchors every heart-rate-based training prescription, from cardiac rehab to elite endurance work. Four age-based estimation formulas dominate the sports-medicine literature: the legacy Fox formula (220 − age, accuracy roughly ±10–12 bpm and known to overestimate in adults under 40 and underestimate over 60), the Tanaka 2001 equation (208 − 0.7 × age, validated on 18,712 subjects and endorsed by Mayo Clinic as the most accurate population-level estimate), the Gellish 2007 equation (207 − 0.7 × age, derived from a 25-year longitudinal cohort), and the Inbar 1994 equation (205.8 − 0.685 × age, preferred for trained athletes). HRmax matters because it converts an abstract intensity prescription into a number on your chest strap or watch: aerobic base work lives at 60–80% HRmax, lactate threshold at 80–90%, and VO2max/anaerobic intervals at 90–100%. The catch is individual variability of ±15 bpm at any age — genetics, training history, β-blockers, and disease all shift the true value. Use a formula as the starting point; refine it with a graded exercise test or field test.
keyTakeaway: Maximum heart rate by age formula: **HRmax = 208 − 0.7×age (Tanaka 2001)**. More accurate than 220−age across the adult lifespan. Expect ±10–15 bpm individual variability; confirm with a graded exercise test if precise zones matter.
useCases: Zone 2 endurance prescription (60–70% HRmax) for base aerobic development in runners, cyclists and triathletes following 80/20 polarized training
Cardiac rehabilitation post-MI: setting a safe HR ceiling (typically 70–85% HRmax, lower if on β-blockers) for supervised exercise
Weight-loss programming: identifying the 60–75% HRmax 'fat oxidation' zone where substrate utilization favors lipids
Masters athletes (40+): adjusting HRmax estimates from Fox to Tanaka or Gellish to avoid systematically under-training
Lactate threshold and VO2max interval prescription for competitive endurance athletes (80–90% and 90–100% HRmax respectively)
Wearable HR zone calibration (Apple Watch, Garmin, Whoop, Polar) when manufacturer defaults use the outdated 220−age formula
explanation:
## Four HRmax Formulas Compared (Worked Example: 35-Year-Old)

For a 35-year-old, the major estimation equations converge tightly:

- **Fox (220 − age)**: 220 − 35 = **185 bpm**
- **Tanaka (208 − 0.7×age)**: 208 − (0.7 × 35) = 208 − 24.5 = **183 bpm**
- **Gellish (207 − 0.7×age)**: 207 − 24.5 = **182 bpm**
- **Inbar (205.8 − 0.685×age)**: 205.8 − 23.975 ≈ **182 bpm**

At age 35 the spread is just 3 bpm. By age 65 the gap widens: Fox predicts 155 bpm while Tanaka predicts 162 bpm — a 7-bpm gap that meaningfully shifts every zone downstream. This is why the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) and most current sports-medicine guidance favor Tanaka over Fox for adults over 40.

## Karvonen Heart Rate Reserve (HRR) — The More Precise Method

The simple percent-of-HRmax method ignores your resting heart rate. The **Karvonen formula** uses Heart Rate Reserve (HRR), which respects individual fitness:

**Target HR = ((HRmax − HRrest) × intensity%) + HRrest**

Example: 35-year-old, HRmax 183 bpm, HRrest 55 bpm, target intensity 70%:
Target HR = ((183 − 55) × 0.70) + 55 = (128 × 0.70) + 55 = 89.6 + 55 = **145 bpm**

Karvonen produces higher target HRs than %HRmax alone and tracks aerobic fitness improvements better as resting HR drops over a training block.

## Measuring HRrest Correctly

Measure resting heart rate on waking, **before standing up** and before caffeine. Lie still for 5 minutes, then count beats for 60 seconds (or use a wearable's overnight low). Trained endurance athletes typically run 40–55 bpm; sedentary adults 65–80 bpm. A 5–10 bpm rise above baseline often signals fatigue, illness, or overtraining.

## The Five Training Zones (AHA / ACSM Framework)

| Zone | %HRmax | Purpose | Talk Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zone 1 | 50–60% | Active recovery, warm-up | Full conversation |
| Zone 2 | 60–70% | Aerobic base, fat oxidation, mitochondrial density | Full sentences |
| Zone 3 | 70–80% | Aerobic capacity, tempo | Short sentences |
| Zone 4 | 80–90% | Lactate threshold | A few words |
| Zone 5 | 90–100% | VO2max, anaerobic | Single words / none |

## Why Zone 2 Dominates Endurance Training

The **80/20 polarized training** model popularized by Stephen Seiler shows world-class endurance athletes spend ~80% of training volume in Zone 2 and ~20% at Zone 4–5, with very little in the 'gray zone' of Zone 3. Zone 2 builds mitochondrial density, capillarization, and fat oxidation without significant central nervous system fatigue — letting you accumulate volume sustainably. The hard work in Zone 4–5 builds VO2max and lactate clearance. The middle (Zone 3) accumulates fatigue without proportional adaptation.

## Estimating vs Testing True HRmax

**Clinical gold standard**: a graded exercise test (GXT) on a treadmill or cycle ergometer with ECG, supervised by a clinician. Stages last 2–3 minutes with increasing speed/grade until volitional exhaustion. The highest 5-second HR is HRmax. Indicated when HR-based prescription matters clinically (cardiac rehab, athletic performance contracts).

**Field test (recreational athletes)**: after a thorough warm-up, perform **3–4 × 4-minute all-out hill repeats** with 3-minute recoveries. The peak HR during the final repeat approximates HRmax within 2–3 bpm. Not appropriate for anyone with known or suspected cardiovascular disease without medical clearance.

## Individual Variability — Why Your Number May Differ

A single age-based formula explains roughly 75% of HRmax variance; the remaining 25% comes from genetics, sex, training status, autonomic tone, and medications. Specific modifiers:

- **β-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol)**: reduce HRmax by 20–30 bpm typically; use RPE (Borg 6–20 scale) or the talk test instead of HR zones
- **Atrial fibrillation**: HR-based prescription is unreliable due to irregular rhythm — use RPE
- **Chronotropic incompetence**: failure to reach 85% predicted HRmax during a GXT despite maximal effort
- **Trained endurance athletes**: often have lower HRmax than predicted (cardiac remodeling) but the formulas still bracket the true value
- **Caffeine and stimulants**: can elevate submaximal HR by 5–10 bpm without changing HRmax

## Wearable Accuracy

Chest strap monitors (Polar H10, Garmin HRM-Pro, Wahoo Tickr) use electrical ECG-style detection and reach **≥95% accuracy** vs lab ECG across all intensities. Wrist-based optical (PPG) sensors — Apple Watch, Garmin Forerunner, Whoop, Fitbit — are within ±5 bpm at rest and light intensity but degrade at high intensity, during interval transitions, and with wrist flexion (push-ups, cycling brake hoods). For Zone 4–5 work or VO2max intervals, a chest strap is the right tool.

## Final Notes

This calculator returns estimates appropriate for training planning. It does not replace medical evaluation. Anyone with known cardiovascular disease, chest pain, syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, or new exercise intolerance should see a physician before maximal-effort testing or high-intensity training. All values reviewed against 2026 ACSM and AHA guidance.

faq.a: Not really. The Fox formula (220 − age) overestimates HRmax in adults under 40 by 5–10 bpm and underestimates in adults over 60 by a similar margin. Tanaka 2001 (208 − 0.7×age) was validated on 18,712 subjects and is the current population-level standard. Use Fox only if you want a rough mental shortcut.

faq.q: My Zone 2 heart rate feels too easy — am I doing it wrong?
faq.a: Zone 2 (60–70% HRmax) is supposed to feel conversational. If you can speak in full sentences and your nasal breathing is comfortable, you're in the right place. Most trained athletes underestimate how easy Zone 2 should feel — that's exactly why 80/20 polarized training works: the easy work has to be genuinely easy to allow the hard work to be genuinely hard.

faq.q: Are wrist-based heart rate monitors accurate during workouts?
faq.a: Optical wrist sensors (Apple Watch, Garmin, Whoop, Fitbit) are within ±5 bpm at rest and Zone 1–2 but lose accuracy at Zone 4–5, during interval transitions, and with wrist flexion. For threshold and VO2max work, a chest strap (Polar H10, Garmin HRM-Pro) is ≥95% accurate vs lab ECG and is the right tool. For Zone 2 endurance and daily HRV tracking, wrist-based is fine.

faq.q: Do β-blockers affect my maximum heart rate?
faq.a: Yes — meaningfully. Metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol and similar β-blockers typically reduce HRmax by 20–30 bpm. HR-based zones become unreliable. Use the Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (6–20 scale) or the talk test instead. Target Borg 12–14 for moderate intensity, 15–17 for vigorous. Always coordinate with your cardiologist.

faq.q: How can I test my true HRmax safely?
faq.a: Clinical gold standard is a graded exercise test (GXT) with ECG supervision — required if you have any cardiovascular risk factors. For asymptomatic recreational athletes cleared for vigorous exercise, a field test of 3–4 × 4-minute all-out hill repeats with 3-minute recoveries reaches within 2–3 bpm of true HRmax. Warm up thoroughly. Don't attempt this without medical clearance if you have any history of chest pain, syncope, or known heart disease.

faq.q: Is spending time at Zone 5 dangerous?
faq.a: Brief Zone 5 intervals (90–100% HRmax, typically 30 seconds to 4 minutes) are how you build VO2max and are well-tolerated by healthy trained adults. Risk rises with cumulative weekly volume in Zone 5 and with pre-existing cardiac disease. Most evidence-based prescriptions cap Zone 5 at roughly 5–10% of total weekly training time. Sustained Zone 5 (>5 minutes continuous) is rarely possible and not the goal.

faq.q: Does HRmax inevitably drop with age?
faq.a: Yes, but training history modulates the slope. Cross-sectional data shows roughly 0.7 bpm decline per year on average. Endurance-trained masters athletes preserve HRmax slightly better than sedentary peers, but the age-related decline is biological (sinoatrial node fibrosis, reduced β-adrenergic responsiveness) and not fully preventable. What you can preserve with training is VO2max and lactate threshold — both far more functionally important than HRmax itself.

faq.q: Should I use Karvonen or percent-of-HRmax for zones?
faq.a: Karvonen (heart rate reserve) is more individualized because it accounts for resting heart rate. It produces higher target HRs than %HRmax alone and tracks aerobic fitness improvements as resting HR drops with training. For most recreational athletes, either method works if applied consistently. For cardiac rehab and clinical settings, Karvonen is preferred.
